body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students explain that a sample can give information about a population when it is representative, and that random sampling tends to produce representative samples (7.SP.A.1).
- Students use data from random samples to make inferences about a population and judge how much estimates vary between samples (7.SP.A.2).
- Students informally assess the overlap of two distributions with similar variability, expressing the difference between centers as a multiple of a measure of variability (7.SP.B.3).
- Students use measures of center and variability from random samples to draw informal comparative inferences about two populations (7.SP.B.4).

MATERIALS
- What Can a Sample Tell Us? (student overview)
- A paper bag of 200 colored beans or tiles (with a known share of one color) for repeated sampling
- A class roster with numbers and a random number generator or numbered slips
- Dot plot templates and sticky dots
- Calculators

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read What Can a Sample Tell Us? Debate: would a survey of the chess club tell us the whole school's favorite lunch? Lesson: Good Samples, Fair Conclusions.
Day 2: Each pair draws a random sample of 20 beans from the bag and estimates the share of red. Plot every pair's estimate on a class dot plot to see sampling variation. Begin Making Inferences from Samples.
Day 3: Finish Making Inferences from Samples. Discuss: why do larger samples give estimates that vary less?
Day 4: Mean and MAD. Make side-by-side dot plots of two data sets and count how many MADs apart the means are. Comparing Two Groups.
Day 5: Assessment: Statistics Check. Students who finish early plan a random-sample survey question for the school.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give a MAD table with columns for value, distance from the mean and total. Use small data sets of whole numbers first.
- Support: offer a sentence organizer for inferences: sample result, fraction or percent, scale up to the population, caution about variation.
- Stretch/Extension: collect real class data (for example, minutes of sleep), take several random samples of 5 and of 15, and show which sample size gives less variable means.
- Multilingual learners: pre-teach population, sample, random, biased, representative, estimate, mean, variability and overlap with a picture of a large group and a small circled group. Provide the frame "Group ___ is typically ___ than group ___, because ___."

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This unit, your child is learning how surveys and polls work: how a small random sample can tell us about a whole group, and why some samples are unfair. When you see a headline like "Most people prefer...", ask your child: Who was asked? How many? Were they chosen at random? These are the questions good data readers ask.
title: Teacher guide: Unit 7: Statistics and Sampling
